items.summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). items.summary: We present a complete, self-contained analysis of the one-loop functional renormalization group (FRG) flow of Quantum Distortion Gravity (QDG), a metric-affine framework with gauged Weyl symmetry. We derive the classical foundations from first principles: the irreducible decomposition of the distortion tensor with an explicit inversion of the trace matrix, the Weyl-covariant distortion $\tilde D$, the no-go theorem for bare distortion invariants, and the Weyl-invariant ultraviolet action with distortion entering through $\phi^2 I_i[\tilde D]$. We then establish the constraint structure of the truncated theory (8 physical degrees of freedom, no spin-2 ghost) via a complete Dirac--Bergmann analysis, and analyze the BRST--BV quantization of the gauge algebra $Diff(\mathcal M) \ltimes Weyl$, including the antifield spectrum, the nilpotency proof, and the classical master equation. We compute the Weyl anomaly coefficients from heat-kernel data and prove the anomaly is cancellable by a Wess--Zumino term. In the main part of the paper we derive all one-loop beta functions from first principles, keeping every intermediate step. We show that in unitary gauge, the dilaton is a gauge mode and does not contribute; Proca fields contribute with three transverse polarizations and no Faddeev--Popov ghosts; Dirac fermions contribute via the Litim fermionic regulator. We extract the matter coefficients $a_S = +1/2$, $a_D = -2$, and $a_V = +3/2$ (the last for a Proca vector in unitary gauge), and we verify each by two independent routes. We derive the gravitational anomalous dimension from the explicit trace over TT graviton, trace mode, and Faddeev--Popov ghosts, reproducing the Litim result $A(\lambda)$ and $B(\lambda)$, and we display the ADM decomposition that yields the mode multiplicities. We show that the fixed-point equation $\beta_{\tilde G} = 0$ is genuinely quadratic in $\tilde G$ at fixed $\lambda$, we solve it explicitly, and we give the resulting discriminant. For the Standard Model matter content ($n_f = 3$, $n_V = 2$), we find a non-trivial UV fixed point at $\tilde G^* \approx 0.43$, $\lambda^* \approx -0.02$, with two relevant directions in the $(\tilde G, \lambda)$ sector, and we compute the stability matrix, critical exponents, and their numerical uncertainties. We verify robustness with a sensitivity scan, showing the fixed point exists for all $C_{\rm bl} > C_{\rm bl}^{\rm crit} \approx -1.02$, well above the QDG value $C_{\rm bl} = -3/(2\pi) \approx -0.477$; we give the analytic form of the critical line. We also analyze the heat kernel in a background field strength $F_{\mu\nu}$, showing that the mixing between graviton and Proca in the $(h^{01}, V^1)$ sector gives a negative contribution to the FRG coefficient $\hat c_V$ (distinct from the Weyl-anomaly coefficient $c^{\rm W}$), and we exhibit the second-order heat-kernel trace explicitly. Finally, we discuss scale generation via Coleman--Weinberg in a two-scalar extension, derive the flat-direction condition, and compare our results with the recent Proca--gravity fixed point of Pastor-Marcos et al. All symbolic and numerical calculations are performed in Python (SymPy, NumPy, SciPy), and the complete code is provided in the appendices, together with additional verification scripts.

items.summary: Berggren's three matrices generate the tree of primitive Pythagorean triples and preserve the quadratic form x₁² + x₂² − x₃². Cha, Nguyen and Tauber (2018) built such trees for other integral ternary forms Q of signature (2,1). We ask whether the matrices alone determine Q. Main results: Recovery criterion (Theorem 3.1). A set of isometries of Q determines Q up to scale exactly when no nonzero vector is sent to plus or minus itself by all of them. Equivalently, the group they generate is not virtually abelian; for integral isometries, it acts irreducibly. The proof is elementary linear algebra and applies to arbitrary real groups. Berggren trees (Theorem 3.2, Proposition 3.3, Remark 3.5). Any two generators determine Q in Berggren's tree and in each of the five trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber. The definition of a Berggren tree alone does not force this: the generators A and A² give a Berggren forest for x₁² + x₂² − x₃² whose two generators both yield edges but do not determine Q. Roots at a rational null line (Theorem 3.6). For a primitive null vector P with divisor G, the minimum of Q on (P^⊥ ∩ ℤ³) \ ℤP is S = |det(2J)|/(2G²). An explicit congruence, Gm ≡ −τ (mod S), decides which minimal vectors e + mP are roots. N-cusps (Theorems 3.7–3.8, Corollary 3.9). For Q = ax₁² + bx₁x₂ + cx₂² − Nx₃² with D = b² − 4ac < 0, all data at the null vectors (p, q, 1) are explicit. A minimal root exists there if and only if gcd(G, S) divides D/G, and in particular whenever D is cube-free. Recovery by integral reflections (Theorem 3.12, Proposition 3.13). Minimal roots at two or three distinct rational null lines yield three integral reflections that determine Q. The paper also relates the reflections in the trees of Cha, Nguyen and Tauber to minimal roots (Remark 3.17), and states an open question for trees produced by their construction.

items.summary: Abstract We present a comprehensive, universal, abstract group-theoretic, module-theoretic, and category-theoretic formalization of bijectively separated rank arithmetic . Given an arbitrary family of algebraic groups {Gi}r i=1 and elements Pi ∈ Gi with finite multiplicative orders oi = ord(Pi), we establish that the additive rank-coordinate space A(P) = Qri=1 Z/oiZ is canonically isomorphic to the external direct product of cyclic power orbits G(P) = Qri=1⟨Pi⟩ under the coordinate evaluation map ΦP(([ni]oi)i) = (Pnii)i. We prove that coordinatewise multiplication in the multiplicative state space corresponds strictly to coordinatewise addition of discrete expo- nent rank classes without introducing analytic logarithms, continuous curves, branch cuts, or topological ambiguities. We extend this framework to general category- theoretic limits, establishing that sub-space coordinate projections and factor permutation reindexings form natural transformations in the category of groups Grp. Furthermore, when lane outputs collapse into a single target background group H, we isolate the exact relation subgroup KP =ker(ΨP) and prove the quotient isomorphism A(P)/KP∼= ⟨P1, . . . , Pr⟩ ≤ H, measuring the precise algebraic information lost during scalar collapse. Finally, we formulate the extension to infinite complex power orbits , polynomial root reconstruction via Newton symmetrization of ranked power arrays Pr ∈ Cr×r, Chinese Remainder Theorem grid decompositions over composite moduli, native linear rank complexity bounds Θ(m), and an axiomatic minimal proof assistant kernel . Keywords: Abstract algebra, cyclic groups, direct products, exponent coordinates, re- lation lattices, projection functors, natural transformations, Newton identities, Chinese Remainder Theorem, rank complexity. items.summary: We give an explicit convex polygon with 63 rational vertices whose area, after its shortest closed Euclidean billiard length is normalized to one, is smaller than that of Mallée’s parabolic triangle. This disproves Conjecture 2.2 of Balitskiy, Mitrofanov and Polyanskii (2026). The polygon was found by moving supporting lines near the parabolic triangle’s focal contacts and then discretizing the resulting shape. The proof checks the literal polygon in exact rational arithmetic: 63 width directions and all 39,711 triples of supporting edge lines. A three-file verification package contains the coordinates and an independent checker. The result identifies a better competitor, without claiming that it is optimal.
items.title: A rational polygonal counterexample to the Mallée parabolic triangle conjecture

items.summary: The Olist Transactional Evidence Benchmark (OTEB) is a neutral, derived research dataset for evaluating analytical methods under incomplete, conflicting, ambiguous, and reconstructable transactional evidence. OTEB is derived from the Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist . It provides a frozen reference cohort of 94,791 internally reconciled orders, 901 deterministic controlled instances, transaction-instance membership, evaluator-only oracle states, and state-specific monetary exposure. The benchmark represents four evidence states: `CONFIRMED`, `RECONSTRUCTED`, `CONFLICTING`, and `UNRESOLVED`. Controlled families cover missing evidence, hard conflicts, unique reconstruction, ambiguous reconstruction, duplicate evidence, and mixed corruption at 5%, 10%, 20%, 30%, and 40%. This release contains the reference oracle, controlled-instance definitions, compact membership index, exposure tables, data dictionary, provenance documentation, reconstruction code, validation code, manifests, schema catalog, and checksums. It contains no method predictions, comparative performance results, ablation studies, paper drafts, dashboards, or private Rahaskin data. Raw Olist CSV files are not redistributed and must be obtained from the original Kaggle source. Original source citation: Olist, & Sionek, A. (2018). items.summary: This repository provides the compiled analysis inputs, R code, figure source data and GIS rasters supporting the manuscript “Historical introduction pools pre-structure future plant invasion debt under climate change”. Version 2.0 contains the final USA-intersection climatic-analogue reconstruction and its corresponding model predictions and spatial summaries. The historical introduction pool contains 18,562 species. The stage-transition models use 5,791 complete-case species, of which 4,088 species without a recorded invasion form the future candidate invasion-debt subset. Future predictions cover 12 combinations of two climate scenarios (SSP126 and SSP585), three periods (2041–2060, 2061–2080 and 2081–2100), and two global climate models (HadGEM3-GC31-LL and MPI-ESM1-2-HR). The archive contains: • Figure_data: XLSX source workbooks for main Figures 1–4, Supplementary Figures S1–S4 and Supplementary Tables S1–S15, together with the compiled species-level analysis dataset and current and future candidate-species predictions. • Code: R scripts, computational inputs and provenance documentation for the stage-transition models, climatic-analogue searches, future predictions, phylogenetic null analysis, temporal analyses, sensitivity analyses and publication source tables. • GIS_rasters: GeoTIFFs for the main and supplementary spatial figures. Main Figure 4 rasters contain sums within globally aligned 0.5° display cells; supplementary spatial rasters retain the native 10-arc-minute resolution. • Validation: execution records and numerical checks. • README files: instructions for reproducing the analyses, plotting the source data and interpreting the spatial fields. Current and future closest US climatic analogue cells are identified separately for each candidate species. POT is the sum of future predicted invasion probabilities assigned to future analogue cells. CHG is future grid-level transition potential minus current grid-level transition potential, with unassigned cells completed with zero. CHG therefore incorporates both changes in predicted probability and relocation of climatic analogues. POSDP is the sum of positive species-level changes assigned to future analogue cells; Supplementary Figure S3 reports its range across the two climate models. The analytical workflow was tested with R 4.3.3. Reproduction starts from the compiled historical master dataset, supplied phylogenetic inputs, prepared species climatic centroids and extracted WorldClim grid values. The package does not independently repeat every upstream archive-curation decision, manual stage-status assignment, GBIF download or occurrence-cleaning step. These boundaries and the optional XLSX and GeoTIFF export procedures are documented in the README. The historical count of 15,950 candidate invasion-debt species is retained for historical summaries; it is not the population used for future predictions. This release supersedes the earlier spatial outputs based on a rectangular climate-search domain. Future results should be interpreted as conditional model projections rather than evidence of a statistically established climate-driven increase in invasion. The repository record is distributed under CC BY 4.0. The software license included in Code/LICENSE and the original terms of third-party inputs remain applicable.

items.summary: GradLint is a fast, standalone Rust-based command-line tool and Python package for diffusion MRI gradient-table quality control. It audits FSL and MRtrix gradient schemes, detects b-vector flip and axis-permutation errors using DWI image evidence, and writes corrected gradient tables with machine-readable provenance. GradLint is designed as a QC gate before diffusion MRI preprocessing, reconstruction, or tractography pipelines. It checks whether the supplied gradient table is geometrically consistent with the diffusion image, reports scheme-quality issues such as shell structure, direction counts, b0 handling, non-unit b-vectors, and angular sampling, and identifies silent convention errors that can otherwise propagate into tensor fitting and tractography results. The core detection method ranks signed axis permutations of the gradient table by a fibre-coherence criterion derived from a diffusion tensor fit. Candidate conventions are evaluated in the appropriate image or world frame for the input format: FSL bvec/bval tables are treated as image-relative, while MRtrix .b tables are treated as world-coordinate gradients. When a high-confidence correction is found, GradLint can emit repaired FSL and/or MRtrix gradient files together with JSON provenance describing the decision, transform, inputs, and outputs.  The software is implemented as a Rust core with thin command-line and Python interfaces. The Python package exposes the same functionality as the CLI and can render JSON reports to Markdown or HTML. Input gradient files are never modified in place unless an explicit overwrite option is used. This record archives the source code for GradLint v1.1.6, corresponding to the GitHub release published on 2026-10-03. The archived source includes the Rust core, CLI, Python bindings, report rendering layer, tests, CI/release metadata, and example materials included in the public source tree. items.summary: This chapter develops the research programme of Generative Relational Economics (GRE) by translating the conceptual, methodological, and substantive architectures developed earlier in the book into a cumulative, contestable, and revisable programme of inquiry. Its principal concern is answerability: GRE claims should specify what is being investigated, what kinds of evidence can support them, what would count against them, which methods are appropriate to their objects, and under what conditions their scope, formulation, or status should change. The chapter first distinguishes the epistemic status of GRE claims and establishes a modular research architecture. It then formulates research programmes for relational economic structures, allocation, heterogeneous value, value conversion and circulation, generative return, generative spacetime, fast–slow dynamics, economic power, justice, generative exploitation, epistemic economy, and AI-mediated capability asymmetry. These substantive programmes are complemented by domain studies, formal modelling, historical and interpretive inquiry, quantitative and empirical research, comparative theory, institutional experimentation, measurement analysis, counterevidence, negative results, replication, reinterpretation, and research infrastructure. A recurring concern is to prevent operationalization from collapsing the distinctions that motivate GRE. Measurement is therefore treated as a transformation with possible loss and reflexive effects; formalization is treated as task-relative rather than as evidence of ontological commitment; justice research keeps normative premises explicit; power and exploitation require mechanism-level identification rather than inference from asymmetry alone; and cross-domain translation preserves non-equivalence and domain-specific remainders. Failed models, failed translations, null results, counterexamples, and negative evidence are treated as constitutive resources for cumulative research rather than as residuals to be discarded. The chapter concludes by specifying how GRE may interact with neighboring Generative Relational domains while retaining disciplinary containment. Candidate cross-domain structures remain hypotheses for further inquiry rather than presumptive components of a completed general theory. GRE thereby emerges not as a closed theoretical system, but as an open research programme whose concepts, methods, models, and domain claims remain historically situated, empirically answerable, formally inspectable, and institutionally revisable.

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).

items.summary: We give an explicit convex polygon with 63 rational vertices whose area, after its shortest closed Euclidean billiard length is normalized to one, is smaller than that of Mallée’s parabolic triangle. This disproves Conjecture 2.2 of Balitskiy, Mitrofanov and Polyanskii (2026). The polygon was found by moving supporting lines near the parabolic triangle’s focal contacts and then discretizing the resulting shape. The proof checks the literal polygon in exact rational arithmetic: 63 width directions and all 39,711 triples of supporting edge lines. A three-file verification package contains the coordinates and an independent checker. The result identifies a better competitor, without claiming that it is optimal.
items.title: A rational polygonal counterexample to the Mallée parabolic triangle conjecture

items.summary: Abstract: Efficient sensing remains critical in low-cost Internet of Things (IoT) and Web of Things (WoT)-enabled edge nodes, even when the sensor itself is inexpensive and widely used. The DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor employs a single-wire dig-ital protocol and relies on Arduino libraries for data acquisition, timeout handling, and scheduling behavior. In this paper, eight Arduino DHT11 libraries are benchmarked on an Arduino Uno R3 using six criteria: flash memory usage, SRAM consumption, average measured call duration, timing variability, maximum CPU blocking time, and failure-recovery behavior. The results reveal substantial performance trade-offs. Aver-age measured call durations ranged from 5,588 µs for the asynchronous DHT Sensors Non-Blocking implementation to approximately 1.04 s for DHT11; however, these measurements reflect different execution semantics and should not be interpreted as directly equivalent end-to-end acquisition latencies. Flash usage ranged from 4,288 to 5,244 bytes, while SRAM consumption ranged from 238 to 266 bytes. TroykaDHT and SDHT delivered the most stable low-latency readings, DFRobot_DHT11 minimized SRAM usage, and DHT Sensors Non-Blocking was most suitable when asynchronous execution and reduced continuous CPU occupation were required. This study does not directly benchmark application-layer protocols or cloud services, such as HTTP, MQTT, REST, or WebSocket; instead, it characterizes sensing-layer behavior that can influence data freshness, task scheduling, and overall responsiveness in resource-constrained IoT/WoT edge deployments.
items.title: Performance Analysis of Arduino DHT11 Sensor Libraries for Resource-constrained IoT/WoT Edge Nodes.

items.summary: This chapter develops the research programme of Generative Relational Economics (GRE) by translating the conceptual, methodological, and substantive architectures developed earlier in the book into a cumulative, contestable, and revisable programme of inquiry. Its principal concern is answerability: GRE claims should specify what is being investigated, what kinds of evidence can support them, what would count against them, which methods are appropriate to their objects, and under what conditions their scope, formulation, or status should change. The chapter first distinguishes the epistemic status of GRE claims and establishes a modular research architecture. It then formulates research programmes for relational economic structures, allocation, heterogeneous value, value conversion and circulation, generative return, generative spacetime, fast–slow dynamics, economic power, justice, generative exploitation, epistemic economy, and AI-mediated capability asymmetry. These substantive programmes are complemented by domain studies, formal modelling, historical and interpretive inquiry, quantitative and empirical research, comparative theory, institutional experimentation, measurement analysis, counterevidence, negative results, replication, reinterpretation, and research infrastructure. A recurring concern is to prevent operationalization from collapsing the distinctions that motivate GRE. Measurement is therefore treated as a transformation with possible loss and reflexive effects; formalization is treated as task-relative rather than as evidence of ontological commitment; justice research keeps normative premises explicit; power and exploitation require mechanism-level identification rather than inference from asymmetry alone; and cross-domain translation preserves non-equivalence and domain-specific remainders. Failed models, failed translations, null results, counterexamples, and negative evidence are treated as constitutive resources for cumulative research rather than as residuals to be discarded. The chapter concludes by specifying how GRE may interact with neighboring Generative Relational domains while retaining disciplinary containment. Candidate cross-domain structures remain hypotheses for further inquiry rather than presumptive components of a completed general theory. GRE thereby emerges not as a closed theoretical system, but as an open research programme whose concepts, methods, models, and domain claims remain historically situated, empirically answerable, formally inspectable, and institutionally revisable.

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly construct multi-agent workflows that decompose a complex task and assign specialist agents from a pool. However, building such a workflow well remains challenging: how finely to divide the task, which agent to trust with each subtask, and when to create a new specialist are all critical decisions a workflow constructor needs to settle up front. Thus, whether each subtask succeeds remains unknown until the workflow runs. Yet, improving a workflow is costly. Locating a fault usually requires a reference answer, a graded outcome, or a trained assessor, and the fix is applied to the whole workflow through re-execution, re-search, or retraining. We propose InFlowOp, which prices every decision in one label-free cost that weighs how well an agent's competence meets what a subtask demands against how much that agent takes to run. Before execution, InFlowOp bidirectionally determines the granularity of task decomposition and agent assignment following from the cost rather than from a fixed template. During execution, InFlowOp corrects a fault with the cheapest move via the same cost that serves the workflow both as it is built and as it runs. Facing the workflow-level evaluation challenge, we introduce Braid, a benchmark whose tasks require multi-agent coordination beyond single-agent capability. Across various domains and backbones, InFlowOp outperforms single agent baselines by up to $+11.97\%$, achieving $+9.64\%$ with in-flow optimization. Our project page: https://xhguo7.github.io/InFlowOp/.
items.title: Pay for the Fault, Not the Flow: Label-Free In-Flow Multi-Agent Workflow Optimization

items.summary: Reproducing a machine-learning result requires knowing how the experiment was run: the data, the model and its size, the optimiser, the learning rate, the batch size, the number of steps, the hardware and the seeds. This information is scattered through a paper---often only in a table caption or an appendix---and is increasingly extracted automatically by language-model pipelines, whose evaluations report how often they are right. We ask the two questions those evaluations leave open: when a pipeline is wrong, does it know it is wrong; and how much human effort does it take to find out? We build a benchmark of 80 arXiv machine-learning papers and annotate 24 of them (240 field decisions), 12 of them through two independent annotation passes, carrying verbatim, line-numbered evidence for every reported and every absent field; the passes agree on 97.5% of presence/absence decisions (Cohen's κ = 0.94), and the residual disagreements are adjudicated under a written scope rule. On that gold standard we run six extraction conditions of increasing agency---a single untruncated prompt, a tool-using agent, schema constraints, table/appendix re-reading, per-field self-assessment with a suspect flag, and mandatory evidence back-linking---over three difficulty strata, 432 full-paper extractions in total. Four results. First, agency buys no accuracy: present recall varies by one percentage point across all six conditions (0.883–0.894) while wall-clock time varies threefold. Second, honesty is a different quantity: 92% of the 387 wrong values were returned without any indication of doubt, and the share of returned values that are silently wrong falls from 12.7% to 5.5% only in the condition asked to flag its own doubts; requiring an evidence quote for every value restores the silent rate to 11.2% because it crowds out the doubt flag. Third, the errors are not inventions: every returned value that carries a checkable anchor occurs somewhere in the paper, and 375 of the 387 errors are values the document does contain—misattributions that belong to another configuration, another table, or the reference list, or values lifted from elsewhere in the paper—which is why a gold-standard-free anchor audit detects none of them (we report that as a negative result, with the five PDF text-layer artefacts it originally fired on pinned as a 22-case regression test). Fourth, human verification is the binding cost and it is predictable: verifying one field by hand requires a median of 12 candidate passages (up to 273; 4,707 in total for the gold sample) against one passage with an evidence link, although 4 of 25 spot-checked links failed adjudication, three of them because the quoted line does not hold the value. All corpus, prompts, gold annotations, adjudication records, raw runs, per-item API costs and analysis scripts are released with the paper, together with a per-session cost ledger ( runs/session-costs.json : the grid itself cost $2.84, the 644 sessions recorded in the released artefacts cost $3.22).

items.summary: We give an explicit convex polygon with 63 rational vertices whose area, after its shortest closed Euclidean billiard length is normalized to one, is smaller than that of Mallée’s parabolic triangle. This disproves Conjecture 2.2 of Balitskiy, Mitrofanov and Polyanskii (2026). The polygon was found by moving supporting lines near the parabolic triangle’s focal contacts and then discretizing the resulting shape. The proof checks the literal polygon in exact rational arithmetic: 63 width directions and all 39,711 triples of supporting edge lines. A three-file verification package contains the coordinates and an independent checker. The result identifies a better competitor, without claiming that it is optimal.
items.title: A rational polygonal counterexample to the Mallée parabolic triangle conjecture

The Full benchmark comprises 4,000 run-level observations obtained from 100 repetitions for each combination of five optimization methods and eight gateway budgets (k = 3–10). Repository contents Python source code and computational validation utilities. Nine original CSV files containing experimental observations, aggregated statistics, evaluation effort, and optimizer provenance. OpenStreetMap territorial input ( sunny3.osm ). Forty scientific figures in PDF format. Installation and execution instructions using Anaconda. SHA-256 file-integrity manifest and licensing information. The archived results support independent verification of the reported statistics and new computational experiments. The original historical environment metadata and detailed event histories are not included; therefore, bit-for-bit replay of the historical execution environment is not claimed. N−1 resilience represents gateway-access service retention and does not certify fault-tolerant physical-backbone connectivity. This software and dataset are released to support transparent computational research, independent assessment, and further development of resilient urban Internet of Things infrastructure planning.

The audio-only comparison is the acoustic branch of the same SaudiDID-X training run , not an independently trained model. The archived test macro-F1 values are 52.01% for the audio-only branch and 53.79% for SaudiDID-X. The release includes analysis and reference-training notebooks, configuration metadata, anonymized split identifiers, text-free per-utterance result artifacts, statistical-test outputs, figures, tables, checksums, and a verification script. It preserves positive, negative, and inconclusive findings, including positional-confounding controls and comparisons with alternative length-control strategies. The work distinguishes prediction of generation termination from semantic reasoning completion: a decodable near-end signal or a reduction in output length does not, by itself, establish that reasoning is complete. items.summary: Abstract   The Universal Research System with Reverse Itinerary (SUII) is a retrospective analytical methodology designed to reconstruct, in a traceable and auditable manner, the probable pathway leading from an initial problem or question to a completed scientific product. This manual brings together the universal prompt, a mandatory common core, ten core modules—including bibliographic analysis (SUII-B)—and six specialised extensions: journalistic and opinion texts (SUII-P), audiovisual or audio documents (SUII-AV), legislation and regulatory documents (SUII-L), case law and judicial decisions (SUII-J), critical appraisal of scientific articles (SUII-LC), and traceable research information management for datasets and research data objects (SUII-TRIM). Each module guides the extraction of locatable traces, classification of the epistemic status of claims, and construction of matrices linking evidence, inference, confidence, alternatives, and required verification. SUII-TRIM extends this logic to the provenance, versioning, transformation, quality control, preservation, access, and reuse of research datasets, while preserving the distinction between directly observed information, information provided by the researcher, reasoned inference, and non-determinable information. The method separates retrospective reconstruction from the prospective generation of hypotheses and requires rival explanations whenever the evidence does not support a unique conclusion. It also incorporates procedures for methodological auditing, version comparison, conceptual genealogy, peer review, algorithmic-bias assessment, external validation, teaching, and traceable research data management. SUII is not intended to recover the authors’ actual psychological history or to replace validated tools for methodological appraisal, risk-of-bias assessment, certainty of evidence, data stewardship, or repository curation. Its application requires version-controlled corpora, decision logs, retention of prompts and outputs, source verification, preservation of original data objects when applicable, and mandatory human oversight. When the available traces are insufficient, the appropriate result is “not determinable.” The manual provides practical criteria for selecting, combining, and quality-controlling the modules according to the product under analysis and the research objective, while maintaining explicit boundaries between documented evidence, reasoned inference, speculation, and unresolved uncertainty .   Resumen   El Sistema Universal de Investigación con Itinerario Inverso (SUII) es una metodología de análisis retrospectivo orientada a reconstruir, de forma trazable y auditable, el itinerario probable que conduce desde un problema o pregunta inicial hasta un producto científico finalizado. Este manual reúne el prompt universal, un núcleo común obligatorio, diez módulos nucleares y seis extensiones especializadas: análisis bibliográfico (SUII-B), textos periodísticos y de opinión (SUII-P), documentos audiovisuales o sonoros (SUII-AV), legislación y normativa (SUII-L), jurisprudencia y sentencias (SUII-J), lectura crítica de artículos científicos (SUII-LC) y gestión trazable de información y datos de investigación (SUII-TRIM). Cada módulo guía la extracción de huellas localizables, la clasificación del estado epistemológico de las afirmaciones y la construcción de matrices que relacionan evidencia, inferencia, confianza, alternativas y comprobaciones necesarias. El método separa la reconstrucción retrospectiva de la generación prospectiva de hipótesis y exige formular explicaciones rivales cuando la evidencia no permite una conclusión única. items.summary: Data and Python code accompanying the manuscript “Replication-Based Criteria Can Change the Selected Number of Clusters: A Seven-Criterion Audit of k-Means on Indonesian Provincial Environmental Data” (submitted to the Journal of Computing Theories and Applications). The package audits how the number of clusters, k, is selected for k-means on a small tabular dataset: the published components of Indonesia’s Environmental Quality Index (Indeks Kualitas Lingkungan Hidup) for 38 provinces, 2021–2024. Seven criteria are computed for k = 2 to 8: the within-cluster sum of squares (read visually and by two formal knee rules), silhouette width, the Davies–Bouldin and Calinski–Harabasz indices, the gap statistic, subsample stability (adjusted Rand index over 200 pairs of overlapping 80% subsamples) and agreement with Ward linkage. The scripts also run sensitivity analyses, a comparison of six clustering algorithms, fixed-centroid assignment across years, a leave-one-out comparison of regression models for the air quality component, permutation importance and exact Shapley values. Contents: data/ (index components 2021–2024; GRDP per capita and population density; a cell-level provenance audit), code/ (six analysis scripts and a plotting-style module), README.md (run order, variable dictionary and data sources), requirements.txt (pinned library versions), CITATION.cff and licence files. Running the six scripts in the order given in README.md reproduces every table and figure of the manuscript in about four minutes on a laptop (Python 3.11 or later). The indicator values are official statistics from Statistics Indonesia (Badan Pusat Statistik) and are reproduced unchanged. Please cite the original BPS tables as well as this record.
